equivalent: the doc comment above this line already states that `mantissa == 0` alone decides the predicate and that the exponent test is kept as the explicit statement of the rule, not as the deciding clause. The three zero-mantissa exponent classes are: exponent 0, which is +0.0 or -0.0 and is already taken by the `!(x > 0.0)` guard (a subnormal power of two such as 2^-1074 has exactly one mantissa bit SET, so its mantissa is not zero and it is rejected by this clause either way); exponents 1..=2046, which are exactly the positive normal powers of two the predicate exists to accept; and exponent 2047 with a zero mantissa, which is an infinity and is already taken by the `!x.is_finite()` guard. So for every f64 that reaches this line the two expressions agree bit for bit, and no test on any input could tell them apart.

equivalent: `Tensor::new`, which this constructor delegates to on its last line, performs exactly the same `tokens == 0` check first and returns exactly the same value, `Err(AttnError::Empty { what: "tokens" })`. With tokens = 0 the intermediate steps are total: `0usize.checked_mul(channels)` is `Some(0)` for every channels, and `vec![0.0; 0]` is an empty allocation that cannot fail, so nothing panics on the way to that delegated check. The only observable difference the early return could have is on which line the error is constructed, and `AttnError` carries no location. No test could tell the two apart; what the early check buys is the OVERFLOW case (`tokens * channels` past a usize), and that is the `checked_mul` on the line below, which this edit leaves in place.

equivalent: `.max(1)` can never fire. By the time this line is reached the guard above has established x > v_th - v_reset > 0, so x > 0 and the numerator x + v_reset - v_th is strictly positive; therefore r = (x + v_reset - v_th)/x = 1 - (v_th - v_reset)/x lies strictly between 0 and 1, and r.ln() is strictly negative. The tau = 1 case (d == 0) returned earlier and tau >= 1 is enforced at construction, so here 0 < d < 1 and d.ln() is strictly negative too. A negative divided by a negative is positive, so (r.ln()/d.ln()).ceil() is at least 1 for every input that reaches the cast, and the `t > f64::from(u32::MAX)` guard above has already excluded the values where the cast itself would misbehave. `t as u32` and `(t as u32).max(1)` therefore agree on every reachable input and no test could distinguish them.
